Leading the charge on two wheels. While electric scooties may not have much motor power, a bike with peak power of 2,000W can carry heavier loads.—Courtesy NCGCL On a Sunday, a family of five can climb onto a Honda CD 70 in North Nazimabad and head to the beach. On weekdays, the same bike can carry a commuter to work, a child to school and a delivery ride through an entire shift. This is the benchmark electric two-wheelers have to beat in Pakistan. “Essentially, Pakistan is a two-wheeler market,” says Faraz Zaidi, Chairman Wasl Mobility Modaraba which provides financing solutions to underserved sectors, including electric mobility. Around two million motorcycles are sold in Pakistan every year and the total fleet exceeds 30m. The economics of switching to electric are compelling. Before the US attack on Iran, the operating cost of an EV bike was around 25 per cent of that of a conventional bike, including petrol, engine oil, spark plugs and filters. Since the war, it has fluctuated around 15pc, says Mr Zaidi. Electric two-wheelers are cheaper to run than a CD70, but that alone may not be enough to unseat the country’s petrol workhorse But the upfront cost remains a major obstacle. A CD70 costs Rs168,000, while a proper lithium-powered electric bike costs more than Rs300,000. The consumer therefore has to spend considerably more today to save on running costs later. The higher the mileage, the faster the payback from switching from petrol to electricity. In ballpark terms, Mr Zaidi estimates that the additional investment can be recovered in around 1.5 years through fuel savings. Yet adoption remains limited. Last year, around 150,000 electric bikes and scooties were sold across Pakistan. Fewer than 200,000 of the 2m bikes sold annually are now electric, putting the adoption rate at less than 10pc, he says. A fragmented market One of the challenges is the range of options available, some with questionable quality. There are roughly 40 operational original equipment manufacturers making two-wheeler EVs in Pakistan because it is much easier to manufacture a bike than a car, says Ammar Habib Khan, CEO of National Credit Guarantee Company Limited, which is working on a financing model for two-wheeler EVs. One reason demand remains weak is that the market is too fragmented, says Mr Khan. He points to companies such as BYD, which helped build demand for Chinese cars globally by demonstrating that Chinese cars could be good quality at a competitive price. Pakistan’s electric two-wheeler market similarly needs an anchor brand, he argues. The absence of standardisation is another problem. Batteries account for roughly 40pc to 45pc of the cost of an electric bike. For a bike costing Rs200,000, the battery alone can account for around Rs100,000. Battery and motor capacity also determine what the bike can actually do. The greater the load, the faster the battery depletes, increasing range anxiety. Family electric two-wheelers? Parents and children, from babies to teenagers, routinely ride together on motorcycles as a form of family transport. Can an electric two-wheeler serve the same purpose? It comes down to motor power, explains Huma Yahya Khattak, CEO of Elfa, EV Technologies.While electric scooties may not have sufficient motor power, a bike with peak power of at least 2,000 watts can carry a heavier load. But the greater the load, the faster the battery depletes, reducing the range. Road conditions pose another challenge. Electric scooties generally have very low ground clearance, which is poorly suited to Karachi’s roads. This is one reason there are more electric scooties in Lahore than in the port city. The CD70, meanwhile, remains a popular choice because it is reliable and has an established ecosystem of spare parts and maintenance. The electric bike also faces a problem that the CD70 does not: resale value. A bike can lose roughly 50pc of its value once it leaves the showroom, partly because there is no established secondary market for EV bikes and partly because the battery gradually loses capacity, much like the battery of the device on which this article is being read. Battery swapping could help address both the cost and inconvenience of battery degradation. Under the model, the consumer buys the bike but rents the battery, swapping a depleted battery for a charged one. The model has been used successfully in China. The charging problem The operational cost savings of EVs make sense only if the vehicles can be charged easily. A lack of charging infrastructure, combined with the fact that most of Karachi’s residents live in apartments, makes charging electric bikes a significant challenge. Yet consumers are finding ways around it. “Some of our customers have bought good extensions which they toss down from the balcony,” says Ms Khattak. Others have arrangements with homes on the ground floor or nearby kiryana stores. Some charge their bikes at their offices. Businesses are also emerging around the charging problem. ChargePK, an app and community, allows drivers to locate the nearest charger. “There are at most only about 100 DC chargers in Pakistan at the moment,” says Fahad Hassan, founder of ChargePK. “Most people don’t feel comfortable owning an EV because there is a lack of chargers. Even the ones available, not all are reliable.” The app currently has 2,500 users, mostly for cars, and only two for bikes. The problem is not merely the number of chargers. Many DC chargers in Pakistan do not allow bikes, while many bikes do not support the type of DC charging available. This creates an additional hurdle for consumers who cannot charge at home or at work, adds Mr Hassan. ChargePK is also in talks with e-swap technologies that would allow riders to exchange depleted batteries for charged ones. Such technology could be particularly important for delivery riders, for whom a bike is not simply a means of transport but a source of income. Foodpanda is a useful test case. Its riders spend their entire working day on their bikes, making them among the consumers who stand to gain the most from lower running costs. The higher the mileage, the shorter the payback period on an EV. Yet uptake has been slow, says Muntaqa Peracha, CEO of Foodpanda. Only around 150 bikes in a fleet of approximately 40,000 are electric, largely because of charging times. “In the roughly 30 minutes it takes to charge an electric bike, a rider could be out making a delivery as that is approximately the time it takes to complete one order,” says Mr Peracha. Simply put, charging a bike can cost a Foodpanda rider the earnings from one delivery. The supply-side squeeze While sky-high petrol prices following the US attack on Iran have pushed up demand for EVs, the momentum had actually started building in the second half of last year, says Mr Zaidi of Wasl Mobility Modaraba. Ms Khattak agrees, but says the bigger constraint on adoption is now on the supply side rather than the demand side.“The war was a ‘buzz’; demand started before the conflict broke out. However, managing working capital is a challenge.” Electric bikes remain heavily dependent on imports from China, requiring letters of credit and strong credit lines. Without inventory, there can be no sales; without sales, there is not enough cash flow to replenish inventory. At 1,000 units a month per OEM, an assembler must commit around Rs200 million in working capital before a single bike is sold, says Mr Khan. Elfa is a case in point. Ms Khattak says the company “is scrambling to get money to order more material”.Elfa imports completely knocked-down scooters from China and assembles them locally. It also manufactures its own batteries, while importing other components such as motors and controllers. The irony is that the economics of an electric two-wheeler are increasingly difficult to ignore. But in a market where the motorcycle is expected to carry a family, survive poor roads, retain its value and remain available for work all day, low running costs alone may not be enough to persuade Pakistan to give up its petrol-powered workhorse until a stronger ecosystem is in place. Punjab governor directs Aitchison College to frame merit-based selection rules. LAHORE: The Punjab governor has directed Aitchison College to formulate merit-based policies for the selection of college prefects and other student leadership positions in sports and academics. The governor, who is also president of the Aitchison College Board of Governors, in a letter addressed to the college principal on Aug 13, desired that the policies should clearly define the eligibility criteria, selection procedure, tenure, code of conduct, roles and responsibilities and other relevant provisions, to ensure fairness, transparency and uniformity in all appointments, selections and promotions. He also called for ensuring fairness in the appointment of housemasters as well as promotion of academic and administrative staff. The governor also desired that the policies, after obtaining approval of the BoG, be uploaded on the college website and official social media platforms. The Aitchison College Old Boys’ Association (ACOBA) executive committee has, however, strongly rejected the unsubstantiated posts circulating on social media that make serious allegations against the college. Parents allege nepotism in prefect appointments, recommendations for foreign admissions; Old Boys panel rejects charges, defends principal Citing Punjab Governor’s letter, the parents of H2 students, attending the Leadership Camp, had same evening written a letter to Principal Dr Syed Turab Hussain objecting to the appointments of college prefects (CPs), head boys and deputy head boys alleging that they were assigned leadership roles through nepotism and unfair practices.The parents attached two lists of students claiming nepotism used for their appointments as CPs and recommending them for admission to international universities. They alleged the students having poor grades and even those who joined the institution in E2 (Grade 7), were made CPs. In the second list, the parents listed students’ names who were recommended for admission to international universities by the institution’s administration, despite having poor Cambridge A Level Part-I grades. Claiming that there are several such students, the parents have circulated a list of 10 students whose admissions were either placed on probation, on hold, and even cancelled for their poor A Levels final results by the international universities during the previous and incumbent principals’ tenures since 2019.Parents also claimed that many Ivy League universities including Harvard had now blacklisted Aitchison College due to its ‘nepotistic policies.’ The parents demand that steps be taken to remove such students from leadership roles, who do not genuinely merit their positions, to restore integrity. Dawn shared the governor’s letter as well as allegations leveled by parents with principal Dr Turab Hussain, but he opted not to respond directly. Instead, the ACOBA responded to the allegations, including apprehensions against the appointment of the principal, circulating on social media. They also shared their written response with the governor. Rejecting the allegations, the association’s executive committee (EC) members stated that they were standing firmly with the college in upholding the values of transparency, merit, and fairness that Aitchisonians had always taken pride in. Association’s president Usman Haq, general secretary Omer Qureshi and EC members stated the college principal was appointed through an open process advertised in both local and international media, drawing over 120 applications, including candidates from abroad. The interview process was conducted by a search committee comprising a majority of members from outside the BoG and supported by a European reputed global education consulting firm. With regard to the appointment of CPs and college awards, they stated student leadership, college honours, and college awards were the outcome of an established robust process. Explaining the procedures, the association stated that comparable, merit-based processes govern the award of College Colours in sports and Honours in academic and extracurricular activities. Referring to allegations of nepotism in recommending students for admissions to universities abroad, the association first expressed its resentment over naming children publicly. “Their names, futures, and reputations are not material for public spectacle,” the association observed and asserted that the public targeting or exposure of students was wholly unacceptable and it would stand unequivocally and without reservation for their protection and dignity. “The admission committees of leading international universities weigh academics alongside personal essays, standardised test scores, extra-curricular achievements, recommendations, and other factors that are well beyond the college’s realm,” the ACOBA stated. Sindh govt lifts ban on commercial use of residential plots. KARACHI: In a major development that could reshape the city’s long-running battle over land use, the Sindh Master Plan Authority on Friday withdrew the notification that imposed an immediate ban on the conversion of residential land for commercial use, opening the door to a fresh regulatory chapter for Karachi’s property landscape. However, officials said the withdrawal of the notification does not amount to an automatic green light for commercialisation, as any change of land use remains subject to applicable laws, master plans and approvals of the competent authorities. The move, made in compliance with the Federal Constitutional Court’s (FCC) May 2026 order, effectively removes the 2019 Sindh Building Control Authority notification that had frozen changes in land use following the Supreme Court’s orders of 2018 and 2019. The FCC in May 2026 had lifted the ban on the conversion of residential plots to commercial and recreational use in Karachi, providing major relief to builders and developers. Master Plan Authority withdraws notification freezing land-use changes following SC orders of 2018 and 2019; officials say commercialisation ‘subject to applicable laws’ A two-member bench, headed by Justice Aamer Farooq while disposing of the case overturned a previous ruling that prohibited the conversion of residential plots into commercial properties in Karachi. The bench clarified that amenity plots, including parks, hospitals, schools, mosques, playgrounds, and graveyards, cannot be converted for commercial or residential purposes. During the hearing, Justice Aamer remarked that the court would not interfere in the functioning of institutions such as the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA). He further said that the affected parties also have the right to file appeals against the High Court decisions. Justice Aamer also said that the court’s suo motu powers no longer exist and emphasised that laws are already in place to address violations of building regulations. The fresh notification from the Sindh Master Plan Authority marks a significant turn in the city’s contentious land-use regime, coming after the FCC recalled the earlier Supreme Court orders that had formed the basis for the citywide restrictions on conversion of land use. In the notification, the Sindh Master Plan Authority has now formally spelled out the consequential step taken pursuant to the court’s May 12, 2026 order. “With the approval of the Competent Authority and in pursuance of the Order dated 12.05.2026, passed by the Honorable Federal Constitutional Court of Pakistan in C.P.L.A. No. 815-K of 2016, whereby the Orders dated 21.12.2018 and 22.01.2019, passed by the Honorable Supreme Court, together with all directions issued and actions taken pursuant thereto or awaiting implementation, were recalled. Consequently, the notification No. SBCA/PS-CE/2019/01 dated 24.01.2019, issued by the Sindh Building Control Authority in pursuance of the Order dated 22.01.2019, regarding the immediate ban on conversion (change of land use), is hereby withdrawn with immediate effect,” said the notification. “All concerned shall ensure strict compliance with and implementation of the directions contained in the aforesaid Order dated 12.05.2026 of the Honorable Federal Constitutional Court, in letter and spirit.” When contacted senior director of Sindh Master Plan Authority Shakeel Siddiqui, under whose signature the notification was issued, told Dawn that the fresh regime of land use would be “applicable immediately” 12.05.2026 of the Honorable Federal Constitutional Court, in letter and spirit.” When contacted senior director of Sindh Master Plan Authority Shakeel Siddiqui, under whose signature the notification was issued, told Dawn that the fresh regime of land use would be “applicable immediately” after the fresh move from the institution. “The city’s regulation of residential and amenity plots has remained a contentious issue for years, particularly over their conversion for commercial purposes and the expansion of commercial activity into residential areas,” said a former official privy to the affairs of land regulation and real estate business in the city. “The issue gained renewed significance following the Supreme Court’s orders of December 21, 2018 and January 22, 2019, after which restrictions were imposed on changes in land use. The measures had a significant impact on property owners, developers and businesses seeking approval for commercial use or conversion of residential plots.” The FCC order of May 12, 2026, recalling the earlier Supreme Court orders and consequential directions, he added, has brought the long-running legal and regulatory question back into focus. Mineral treasure. OFFICIALS often state that Pakistan’s untapped mineral wealth can be a potential ‘game-changer’. The planning minister’s recent comment while speaking to a think tank in New York, offers more of the same optimism. According to Ahsan Iqbal, Pakistan’s mineral endowment was estimated to be worth “more than $7 trillion”. It is not known how the minister arrived at that eye-watering figure. Mr Iqbal also mentioned that exploiting this mineral wealth required major investment, while the “country’s volatile political climate” was the “primary deterrent” to attracting foreign capital in the sector. In other words, this massive bonanza cannot be tapped just yet. There is little doubt that Pakistan has immense untapped mineral wealth, including critical minerals, which have become a hot commodity globally due to their use in emerging technologies. Independent assessments have endorsed Pakistan’s mineral potential, although the state’s estimates about the true value of this wealth, and those of third parties, vary considerably. It is also a fact that currently, the mining sector’s contribution to total GDP is miniscule. Pakistan’s lack of funds, expertise and technology are the main impediments standing in the way of exploiting this potential. The Americans have expressed interest in our critical minerals, while the Chinese have also invested in the mining sector. But the biggest obstacle in attracting foreign capital and expertise is the poor security situation in the areas where Pakistan’s mineral wealth is concentrated: Balochistan and KP. The prime need, therefore, is to improve the security situation if the state is serious about foreign investors putting their money into the mining sector. A securitised approach alone will not yield the desired results. As mining activity largely takes place in areas with high poverty, the investment must bring socioeconomic improvements to the lives of the local population. Residents living near mining projects must have first priority where training and jobs are concerned, while those firms profiting from the area should also invest in infrastructure improvement and corporate social responsibility. Moreover, the trend so far has been for investors to dig up raw material and haul it away overseas for value-addition. To create a lasting economic impact, along with extraction, downstream industries are required which are capable of processing and adding value to the raw material. This will help create more jobs. Pakistan’s mineral wealth can bring dividends if it benefits the local people, and helps diversify the economy. Therefore, the state must concentrate on security, community development as well as policy continuity to attract foreign investment to the mining sector. Otherwise, Pakistan’s mineral treasure worth trillions will end up becoming a ‘resource curse’. Published in Dawn, August 29th, 2026

Restructuring CSS. SINCE 1947, approximately 40 commissions, committees and taskforces have attempted to reform Pakistan’s civil service, and the core themes have been remarkably similar: merit over seniority, competitive pay to reduce corruption, better mid-career training, and curbing the dominance of the elite generalist cadre over specialist services. Despite these efforts, bureaucracy has proved stubbornly resistant to change. This is even more urgent amid the current debate on creating new provinces or administrative units, since no attempt to fix systemic governance failures can succeed unless the civil service architecture is reformed first. Layering governance reform onto the bureaucracy as it stands would only expand an already bloated apparatus, without empowering citizens. From the 1950 Gladieux Report and 1962 Cornelius Commission to Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s 1973 reforms, which abolished the Civil Service of Pakistan cadre on paper but stripped away constitutional protections and opened the door to political victimisation, to the Ishrat Husain Commission (2006-08) and successive task forces, each produced recommendations that stalled at implementation, including the 2023-25 Ahsan Iqbal-led committee’s 48 proposals on recruitment, training and compensation. Three interlocking reasons explain this failure: bureaucratic resistance, as the elite DMG/PAS (District Management Group/ Pakistan Administrative Service) cadre arguably undermines reforms, threatening its monopoly over power, perks, and postings; political interference, as leaders favour loyal, compliant bureaucrats over an independent, merit-based administration; and superficial pay reform without touching the underlying structure. Our civil service still largely operates on 1973-era structures. Consequently, our civil service still largely operates on 1973-era structures — defined, sadly, by loyalty, sycophancy, and patronage; distorted compensation for top bureaucrats; civil servants focused on personal welfare; and power with little accountability. Breaking this cycle requires a blueprint that anticipates the resistance which has defeated every commission so far. This article sets out six concrete measures to make Pakistan’s bureaucracy leaner, merit-based, and accountable to the public, not political bosses. First, the nomenclature of CSS (Central Supe­r­ior Services) itself needs to be banished. It inculcates a false sense of superiority and entitlement among civil servants that runs through their ent­i­­re career and defines their condescending behaviour with the public they are supposed to be serving. Second, the all-Pakistan services (PAS and PSP) must be dismantled to tame a stubborn bureaucracy. The record of DMG/PAS officers speaks for itself: introducing distortionary tax policies (such as filer/non-filer regime) as FBR chairmen, designing IPP contracts, planning projects that appear politically motivated, neglecting human development, colluding with donors, and outsourcing economic policy formulation to IFIs. This makes a strong case for dissolving a generalist cadre that claims top positions, and that even intrudes into specialised service groups, based on affiliation rather than competence, thus marginalising economists and technocrats. Importantly, pro­­vinces already run administrative services like the Provincial Management Services performing the same functions. The same logic extends to policing: law and order is a provincial subject, and Pakistan already has provincial police forces, as does every state in the US, county in Britain, and state or region in Australia — hence, there’s no justification for dominating federating units. Third, Pakistan’s trade bureaucracy is both oversized and structurally fractured. Pakistan Customs offers a clean illustration: it employs close to 9,500 personnel, including about 500 gazetted officers in BS-17 to 22, to manage under $100 billion in total trade, while Singapore runs its entire customs operation on roughly 500 to 1,000 staff handling over $1 trillion trade, and South Korea manages $1.341tr with about 5,786 staff. This ratio is wildly out of line with most comparable administrations, and buys no compensating efficiency. Pakistan still extracts roughly 17 per cent of import value in taxes at the border ($16.9bn against $69bn in imports in FY26), reflecting its continued reliance on import-stage taxation rather than broad-based domestic direct taxation or trade facilitation. The fracture compounds the bloat: the Commerce and Trade Group formulates tariff, trade, and investment policy through the commerce ministry, while Pakistan Customs Service executes at the border, enforcing policy orders that CTG itself designs. This separation, historically rationalised as checks and balances, has instead produced policies conceived without operational insight and enforced by officers with no institutional stake in their design. There is a strong case for merging CTG and PCS into a unified ‘Trade and Customs Service’ that aligns authority with accountability. Fourth, public service recruitment needs restructuring around actual job requirements rather than a single generalist gateway. There is no reason recruitment to the postal, railways, information, and military lands and cantonment groups should continue through CSS, as these services have lost relative significance today: Postal and Railways should become autonomous commercial organisations, while the Information Group’s functions are redundant given Pemra already regulates media. More broadly, instead of a gruelling multi-subject syllabus and a two-year cycle, the Federal Public Service Commission should run graduate recruitment programmes tailored to specific jobs: accounting, finance, economics, public policy, law, and IT-trained fresh graduates for Customs and Inland Revenue Service via GRE-type tests, chartered accountants for audit and accounts, and graduates in international relations, development, economics, or relevant studies for the Foreign Service. Currently, MBBS doctors, engineers, and MA in Urdu or Islamic studies land in IRS, Customs, Foreign Service, or Accounts purely on CSS ranking. Fifth, perquisites should be monetised and decent enough to attract the best talent. No advanced country provides government-maintained residences, luxury cars, or personal servants to civil servants, and Pakistan should stop such a drain on public resources. Finally, inducting military officers directly into PAS, Police Service and Foreign Service without the CSS examination should stop. This has long been a shortcut for securing lucrative civil service careers, even as compulsory military attachment for civil probationers usefully builds familiarity with the defence forces. The overarching aim must be a civil service that is citizen- and business-centric, and that possesses the political will to finally act on what several commissions have already told us. The writer is a former CSS officer who holds a PhD degree in economics from the University of Cambridge. CBAM trade barriers. WHILE Pakistan struggles with the accumulated cost of climate inaction and finds international climate finance elusive, it must now confront an emerging challenge: trade barriers priced according to the carbon embedded in each exported product. The false comfort that this does not touch our key exports to the EU and UK has deferred reforms, with the cost growing steeper by the day. Contradictory policy, misusing carbon levies instead of building a domestic Emissions Trading System (ETS), has made trade even harder. Since January 2026, EU importers of steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers and electricity have had to buy certificates for the carbon embedded in their imports, with the first annual declarations due next year. Direct exposure under these sectors is small for Pakistan — roughly 1.2 per cent of total exports, typically a percentage easy to ignore. CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism), however, is a serious warning. On March 9, 2023, my column on ‘Trade and climate adaptation’ in this paper flagged that Pakistan would need to build carbon labelling and export competitiveness around it, not wait it out. As I wrote then, “they are expected to shift demand towards less carbon-intensive products”. Some three years later, in January 2026, my argument turned from a warning to heed to an opening to seize, urging that CBAM “should be seen as an incentive to accelerate our own decarbonisation”. Two columns, three years apart — but one constant: Pakistan’s institutions have moved slower than the mechanism they were warned about. Pakistan’s exports to the EU reached $8.86 billion in FY25, up from $8.24bn the year before, with textiles, which accounted for the largest share of that total, driving the growth. That concentration has real addresses: major textile houses in Faisalabad, Lahore and Karachi — employing thousands of workers and supplying top brands in the EU — are directly exposed in the coming scope expansion. Pakistan’s economic set-up is structured to fund CBAM via citizens’ fuel bills while getting no credit. In the sectors that CBAM already covers, the exposure affects heavy industry: leading domestic cement makers supply most of that sector’s output, with the steel mills in Karachi making up the remainder. The disproportionately higher share, however, sits in textiles, concentrated in three industrial cities that would absorb the shock first. Pakistan already collects carbon levies. CBAM allows a deduction: a home-country carbon price already paid can be subtracted from the EU’s border levy. It is the mechanism’s one window of opportunity — a domestic carbon price that is real, product-linked and verifiable. Pakistan’s misplaced levies cannot qualify because they aren’t earmarked; the revenue funds the deficit, not the industries that generated it. They are regressive, taxing fuel and transport consumption rather than signalling to producers. And they carry no product-level accounting, so a generalised fuel levy tells Brussels nothing about the carbon intensity of a bale of cotton yarn or a tonne of billet steel. Without that link, CBAM won’t recognise it as a carbon price. The cost will fall twice: first domestically into a levy that does nothing for decarbonisation, and then again at the EU border into a certificate purchase. Pakistan’s economic set-up is structured to fund CBAM out of its own citizens’ fuel bills while getting zero credit for it. The Securities and Exchange Commission has draft ESG [Environmental, Social, and Governance] Disclosure Guidelines and the State Bank is building a national Green Taxonomy. The taxonomy lets a bank tell a green loan from an ordinary one; the guidelines let an auditor certify emissions rather than estimating them. Without both at scale, product-level Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) data has nowhere credible to be recorded, and any domestic carbon price has no verified base to attach to. On domestic ETS, the story is older still. In 2018, the climate ministry commissioned a UNFCCC-backed study recommending an ETS for the country’s largest power and industrial emitters — roughly 168 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent. It was never built. What arrived instead was the Carbon Market Policy Guidelines of 2024, aiming at a different problem — a framework for selling carbon credits to international markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, generating revenue from offset projects sold abroad while pricing no carbon at home. Six years after its own study told it what to build, the ministry built something adjacent, and the follow-up never came. No ministry can close this gap alone. Commerce defends market access and negotiates recognition of any domestic carbon price with Brussels. The climate ministry owns the ETS architecture. Industries and production, and finance and revenue carry the implementation weight, ie, audits with textile associations and SMEs, and the decision on whether levies are earmarked. Energy determines whether industrial power and its transmission are clean and cheap enough to matter on a factory floor. A CBAM strategy that lives in a single ministry’s file will not meet the deadline. Fixing this requires no new instrument, only the one Pakistan was already told to build, made legible to the mechanism that is about to tax us anyway. First, earmark a fixed share of carbon and climate levy proceeds by law for a dedicated decarbonisation fund to derisk investments. Second, revive the 2019 ETS design-and-build accredited MRV infrastructure at the product level. Third, sequence deliberately: taxonomy and baseline audit first; verification capacity second; financing (concessional green refinance, green sukuk against industrial assets) third; and only then mandatory disclosure. Get the order wrong, and Pakistan builds compliance infrastructure for a carbon price that still doesn’t exist. None of this is unusual by regional standards. Vietnam did not wait; it used its own EU trade agreement to force pilot emissions trading and SME carbon accounting. Indonesia offers the opposite lesson: a loan-financed energy transition, where debt is now carried alongside the carbon bill — a trap that Pakistan’s fiscal space cannot sustain. The choice facing Islamabad is not whether to pay for carbon; that was decided before the levies were introduced. The choice is whether that payment counts for anything, at home or in Brussels. Right now, it counts for nothing in either place. September 2027 is when this stops being an abstraction and becomes an invoice, priced at EU default values unless Pakistan shows its own numbers by then. The levies can do double duty. Islamabad High Court judge questions legal status of Afghan students. Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro raised questions regarding the legal status of the Afghan students as well as the authority of their lawyer to represent them before the court. During the hearing, the judge questioned the petitioner’s counsel about the circumstances in which the Afghan students were allowed to enter Pakistan and whether similar treatment could be sought by students from other countries. “Sir, we are currently at war with the Afghans. If Indian students come, will you allow them to come too?” Justice Soomro asked the counsel. The lawyer submitted that the 87 Afghan students had arrived in Pakistan in 2023, when, according to him, the national policy regarding Afghan students was different. Justice Soomro observed that the petition had been filed under the constitutional jurisdiction of the high court and questioned whether the Constitution provided Afghan nationals with a right to invoke such jurisdiction. The counsel argued that the students had entered Pakistan on valid student visas for a period of one year and that their presence in the country had been permitted by the government. The judge then questioned the authority under which the lawyer had obtained power of attorney from the 87 Afghan students. “Under which law have you taken power of attorney from these 87 Afghan students?” Justice Soomro asked. The court also suggested that the students should approach the Afghan embassy in connection with their matter instead of seeking relief through the constitutional jurisdiction of the Islamabad High Court. “You should go to the Afghan embassy and your case will be heard there. The Afghan embassy will contact the Pakistani embassy,” the judge remarked. The petitioner’s counsel said that he would assist the court on the legal questions raised during the proceedings. The case concerns the extension of visas of 87 Afghan students who came to Pakistan in 2023 to pursue their studies. The petitioners have sought relief regarding their continued stay in Pakistan following the expiry or impending expiry of their student visas. Trump says US is taking partial control of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, but offers few details about agreement. United States President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unprecedented push to take control of a fifth of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can revive the Opec nation’s battered energy industry while delivering a new source of crude to help bring down US fuel prices. Trump provided few details about the agreement, saying only that the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business. The South American nation’s leader welcomed the agreement, saying it would boost the economy and government revenue. The new deal would represent a dramatic expansion of the US role in Venezuela’s oil industry as the Trump administration seeks to revive the country’s production and secure more crude for US refineries. Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves but produces only about 1.25 million barrels per day, far below its potential after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions. Rubio calls deal a win-win “At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority US control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The announcement followed weeks of US-Venezuelan negotiations over a deal that would give American companies long-term access to a group of Venezuelan oilfields and guarantee the resulting crude supply to the United States. Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week granting new oil exploration and production rights to a number of companies, particularly US firms. Sources have told Reuters that a lease model was under consideration, with fields potentially auctioned to US producers, but the arrangement could face legal and constitutional challenges in Venezuela, where the state retains control over core oil industry activities. Trump did not disclose the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved or how the United States would exercise majority control over the reserves. A list seen by Reuters shows the fields are in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions. Rubio described the agreement as a win for both countries, saying on X that it would secure stable, low-cost oil for the United States and help lower gasoline prices. For Venezuela, Rubio said the deal would bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs and help rebuild the country’s economy. Rodriguez, who became interim leader after the US captured President Nicolas Maduro in January, said late on Friday that the agreement would allow for a significant increase in production through the development of 17 strategic fields and result in tax revenue for the country totaling $209 billion. “These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our countrys economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets,” she said in a statement. Legal basis, financial structure unclear Analysts said they needed to see more details on the agreement’s legal and financial structure before assessing whether it could attract significant investment. Also unclear is whether the deal will lower gasoline prices in the short term, as developing the infrastructure needed to produce, transport and refine Venezuela’s heavy crude could take years. David Goldwyn, president of Goldwyn Global Strategies, said it was unclear whether a US government lease would have a legal basis under Venezuela’s constitution and its new hydrocarbons law, adding that there is “no precedent for having the US government enter into a lease to operate oil fields”. Goldwyn also questioned whether the plan would address the obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela for years. “It is hard to see how this kind of arrangement would accelerate investment at any material scale,” he said, citing political uncertainty, an inadequate power grid, limited export capacity and government discretion over the industry. Since removing Maduro, Washington has been trying to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude for US refineries while promoting American investment in the country’s oil industry. The Trump administration is under pressure ahead of midterm elections in November to mollify consumer concerns over rising gasoline prices. Cheaper oil supplies and expanded output could help. The US also has been looking for solutions to replenish its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the nation’s oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers. Venezuela nationalised its oil industry in the 1970s, putting state-run PDVSA at its centre. Under then-president Hugo Chavez, the government tightened control, forcing foreign producers into state-led joint ventures and later expropriating assets, including projects operated by ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips. Under Maduro’s rule Venezuela’s production fell sharply.

Number of missing in Nepal, China floods soars to nearly 3,000. Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling on Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing villages. The number of missing soared close to 3,000 on Saturday, latest figures from both countries showed, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India. In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash. Those that made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonising wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing. A man takes pictures in front of damaged buildings after flash floods and a mudslide, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters “All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP . Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother. “We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said. ‘Enormous’ trauma The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous”, and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise. Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out. Compounding the search for the missing have been fears of further flooding in affected areas. The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes to form, and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors. Children displaced by flash floods and a mudslide rest inside a relief camp in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location”, saying they had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side”. In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing suspended its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding, before saying the threat had eased. State news agency Xinhua reported early on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the area. ‘All swept away’ On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors. “Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP . Rescuer load relief material in a helicopter to be transported to the areas affected by flash floods and a mudslide as it drizzles at the Maithali Barrack, an army training center, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than a hundred trapped in the same area. Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed. Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck. “The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP . Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday. There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal. Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists — seven people died and 554 remain missing, the state Xinhua news agency reported early Saturday. Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet. In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims. ‘Pilgrimage route’ Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash. Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling by bus with 56 others towards the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam. “Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging towards her. A man walks past a damaged house after the flash floods and mudslide, at Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud. “One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” then scrambled up a hill, she said.

Philippines, UK eye expanded space cooperation, satellite to boost disaster response. The Philippines and the United Kingdom are looking to deepen cooperation in space science and technology, satellite data, artificial intelligence (AI), and innovation, as the two countries prepare for the launch of the Multispectral Unit for Land Assessment (MULA) satellite. Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) Acting Director General Dr. Gay Jane Perez met with United Kingdom Trade Commissioner Martin Kent to discuss MULA's upcoming launch and future opportunities to strengthen bilateral cooperation in space technology applications, according to posts by the British Embassy in the Philippines and PhilSA. The British Embassy said MULA, developed in partnership with the United Kingdom, would support disaster response, agriculture, and environmental monitoring across the Philippines. The satellite is expected to give the Philippines greater capacity to use Earth observation data for disaster risk reduction and management, as well as for monitoring land, resources, and environmental conditions. PhilSA has said MULA will provide data for agriculture, maritime monitoring, disaster risk reduction and management, and national security applications. The agency has also cited the importance of satellite data in disaster operations, including the production of maps showing landslide and earthquake damage, oil spills, burned areas, and flood extents for government disaster response agencies and local governments. PhilSA previously said MULA's higher-resolution imaging capability would allow the country to better monitor terrestrial ecosystems, land and marine resources, agricultural activity, and environmental conditions for more proactive disaster management and mitigation. “From Earth observation to space innovation, the UK and the Philippines are reaching new heights together,” the British Embassy said. Possible 2027 launch MULA, described by PhilSA as the country's most advanced satellite to date, is now fully built and undergoing space environment testing in the United Kingdom to verify that it meets technical and mission-assurance requirements. During the ninth meeting of the Philippine Space Council in June, Perez reported that MULA could be launched in April 2027 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-20, although PhilSA stressed that the development schedule could still change depending on the results of testing. The satellite will carry a TrueColour camera capable of producing 5-meter-resolution images, as well as Automatic Identification System and Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast payloads for detecting and tracking ships and aircraft. “As MULA paves the way for a new era of capability, the UK looks forward to deepening its partnership with PhilSA and advancing even more ambitious space collaborations,” the British Embassy said. UK partnership The UK-Philippines space partnership has been closely linked to MULA's development, with Filipino engineers receiving satellite-development training and hands-on experience from Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd. (SSTL) in the United Kingdom. PhilSA said most MULA engineers have completed intensive know-how transfer and hands-on training with SSTL, allowing them to apply advanced satellite engineering expertise in the Philippines. The agency also previously reported that a UK trade envoy met with PhilSA and MULA engineers in 2022 to discuss the satellite project and opportunities to build more sovereign Philippine satellites in the future. PhilSA's June report said the Philippine Space Council had approved the development of a MULA constellation as a national priority, allowing follow-on satellites to be developed and integrated domestically to ensure more continuous access to Earth-observation data. PhilSA said the initiative would help build a Philippine space industry and establish a nationally owned and operated Earth-observation capability for the country's strategic requirements.

The bond market prepares for a hike to interest rates, while US stocks drift lower. NEW YORK (AP) — The bond market swung Friday as investors built bets that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates soon to get the nation's high inflation under control. U.S. stocks, meanwhile, dipped but not by much after economists said a speech by Chairman Kevin Warsh helped strengthen faith that the Fed will do what's needed to bring inflation down, even if it causes pain for the economy in the short term. The S&P 500 fell 0.2% after flipping between modest gains and losses through the morning. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 9 points, or less than 0.1%, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.5%. The reaction was stronger in the bond market following Warsh's first speech as chairman of the Fed at an annual economic symposium held in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, and the pressure was on Warsh. Worries had grown that his tough talk about getting inflation down to the Fed's 2% target may be just that, unless the Fed backs it up with action. The Fed could hike short-term interest rates to get inflation under control, but it could also feel deterred from doing so because that would slow the economy and hurt prices for investments. And President Donald Trump, who appointed Warsh, has been vocal about wanting interest rates to be lower rather than higher. Warsh was adamant again on Friday that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed plans to do with rates for its two jobs of keeping inflation low and the job market strong. He has said he wants markets to react to what incoming data says about the economy and inflation rather than what the Fed says. But Warsh also said Friday that "short-term interest rates are the predominant tool" for the Fed to do its job. And he said, "I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive," an implication that short-term interest rates may not be high enough to tamp down the economy and inflation. The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for what the Fed will do with its federal funds rate, jumped to 4.35% from 4.22% just before the speech. That's a big move for the bond market, and it was because traders upped their forecasts that the Fed will hike its federal funds rate as soon as next month. They're now betting on a nearly 58% probability of that, up from the 35% seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. Longer-term yields also rose following some initial zigzags, but not by as much as shorter-term yields. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.72% from 4.67% late Thursday, and the 30-year Treasury yield got to 5.21% from 5.19%. All the moves, including the modest ones for stocks even though higher interest rates tend to hurt them, indicate investors "pricing a more credible Fed," according to economists at Bank of America led by Aditya Bhave. "The positive market reaction highlights that investors place a premium on policy clarity, even when that clarity carries" a message implying higher interest rates, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. Yields had gotten so high for longer-term bonds this summer, in part because of worries about inflation staying high in the future, that the U.S. Treasury Department made an unusual move last week and said it would buy back more bonds, though analysts said it will likely have only a limited effect. On Wall Street, Gap jumped 12.9% after the retailer reported stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also said Michael Francis, an industry veteran who began his career on the retail sales floor, will take over as head of its Old Navy stores. Marvell Technology fell 10.3% even though the chip company reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts' expectations. CEO Matt Murphy said its business related to artificial-intelligence technology is strong, and it raised its forecasts for upcoming revenue growth. But analysts said much of that optimism may have already been baked into Marvell's stock price, which came into the day with a surge of 184% for the year so far. After rocketing higher for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks across the industry are confronting skepticism that they shot too high and that booming demand for AI chips may fade if the AI revolution does not produce as much profit as promised. All told, the S&P 500 fell 19.23 points to 7,711.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 9.45 to 53,559.99, and the Nasdaq composite sank 138.93 to 26,402.42. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea's Kospi fell 1.8%, and France's CAC 40 rose 1% for two of the world's bigger moves.

The Cultural Center of the Philippines in the 21st Century. The creation of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or Controlled Corporations (GCG) through R.A. No. 10149 in 2011 marked an important turning point for the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP). Among its significant effects was a stronger emphasis on board accountability and more active board involvement in policy formulation, decision-making, and institutional oversight. The establishment of board committees, prompted by the GCG, has further strengthened governance. These committees have enabled more thorough deliberation of management proposals and board initiatives and have helped make decision-making more informed. Performing arts network The CCP has long worked closely with professional resident companies in music, dance, and drama, and has strengthened its continuing annual events, namely Pasinaya, Cinemalaya, and Virgin Labfest, to which Ternocon, a celebration of Filipino formal wear, was added in 2018. With the closure of the main building, performances have been held at the Metropolitan Theater, the Samsung Performing Arts Theater at the Circuit in Makati City, and elsewhere in Metro Manila and the regions. The outreach program has been active, sponsoring nationwide concerts of the Philippine Philharmonic Orchestra (PPO) and other groups. The PPO has continued to perform abroad, most recently in 10 cities in the United Kingdom. Ayala Land Malls has co-sponsored Metropolitan Opera HD and British National Theatre presentations of grand opera and Shakespeare plays. This resident company network has expanded to include National Performing Arts Companies. More outstanding groups will be added as official CCP partners, creating more opportunities for collaboration. Working with Generations X, Y, Z, and Alpha Venturing beyond the established boundaries of the performing arts, the CCP conceived of Kanto Kultura to encourage the artistically inclined among ordinary young Filipinos. Its first project, Kanto-Kanta, sought to inspire young people to compose and perform using indigenous themes and musical instruments. The concept was simple and accessible: participation was affordable, and the rules were straightforward. The response was enthusiastic, and many of those who took part have since gone on to pursue successful artistic careers. With young audiences and emerging art forms in mind, the CCP also started projects in animation based on selected “Lola Basyang” stories, produced in partnership with De La Salle–College of Saint Benilde. Continuing into new territory, the CCP launched an Animation, Comics and Game Development Grants Program. The results have been encouraging: one grantee, Ranida Games' “Sinag Fighting Game” (inspired by Philippine mythology), has achieved over 900,000 downloads on both Google Play and Apple iOS from numerous players worldwide. To help deepen cultural roots among young Filipinos, initiatives were also taken to revive vanishing arts, notably traditional lullabies. “Himig Himbing: Mga Heleng Atin” was launched in 2022, consisting of audiovisual renditions of eight lullabies based on ethnomusicological research. Professionally arranged and produced, the selections are in Tagalog, Bicol, Kalinga, Subanon, Ilocano, Cebuano, and other Philippine languages. Great art can hardly flourish without an appreciative audience. For creativity to flourish, people must have opportunities not only to experience the arts but also to have the knowledge and ability to understand and appreciate them. The CCP has therefore partnered with the Philippine Normal University (PNU) on a program designed to deepen future teachers’ knowledge and appreciation of culture and the arts. The initiative has a powerful multiplier effect: PNU graduates will eventually teach in schools throughout the country, influencing not only their students but also their fellow educators. In this way, appreciation for the arts can reach far beyond the walls of the CCP and into classrooms and communities nationwide. The visual arts During its first five decades, the CCP devoted much of its attention to music, dance, drama, and film. For the CCP’s second half-century, the board has resolved to give greater prominence to the visual arts, covering painting, sculpture, graphics, photography, and other forms of visual expression. The CCP has an outstanding collection of paintings, musical instruments, and ethnographic items. The painting collection includes the work that introduced modern art to the Philippines, Victorio Edades’ “The Builders,” as well as important works by Amorsolo, Zobel, Joya, and others through the 1980s. Dubbed the 21AM (21st Century Art Museum), it is being digitized and expanded to include more recent works and emerging forms such as installation and video art. More importantly, the CCP hopes to help bring greater international recognition to Philippine visual art and Filipino artists among leading museums and collectors around the world. There are sculptures in various places within the CCP premises, including some by artists from ASEAN countries. These are now arranged on the lawn beside the Philippine Navy Headquarters along Roxas Boulevard. Plans are underway to create a permanent ASEAN sculpture garden within Liwasang Kalikhasan, the tree-covered four-hectare area south of the main building. The Liwasan is planned to be a cultural destination in its own right, with sculpture, fountains, open-air performance areas, perhaps a grove of native flowering trees, and a pool where children can sail miniature boats. It could be a welcoming place where art, nature, recreation, and community can come together. Renovating the CCP main building The renovation of the CCP main building became necessary after more than five decades. Structural and mechanical deficiencies had accumulated, including leaks through the concrete roof, water seepage from below, deteriorating electrical systems, damaged drainage and sanitary facilities, and concerns about the building’s structural integrity. When the CCP was inaugurated in 1969, it ranked among the finest in the world. More than half a century later, however, technology has advanced dramatically. Acoustics, theatrical lighting, stage engineering, audiovisual recording, and production systems have all undergone major transformations. The renovation represents not simply the repair of an aging structure but also an opportunity to equip the CCP for the next generation of artistic production. For the medium term, the complex development plan envisions a separate building for administrative offices not directly required for main building productions. In keeping with this plan, administrative offices will continue to be housed in the CCP Annex. The space released in the main building will therefore be devoted to conference rooms, exhibitions, official reception areas, and other public-oriented functions, helping transform the main building into a destination that visitors will experience as a cultural attraction in its own right. With global warming and a rising population, the CCP is exploring possibilities of building facilities at the Clark Economic Zone. As the CCP looks beyond its historic home, its continuing challenge—and promise—is to ensure that the arts remain a vital, accessible, and evolving part of the nation’s future. Filipina American artist Thea Canlas wins 2026 Sondheim Art Prize. Filipina American artist Thea Canlas has been named the winner of the 2026 Janet and Walter Sondheim Art Prize, receiving the $30,000 award for her work exploring diasporic Philippine identity. Thea was announced as the winner Aug. 27 during an awards ceremony at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore. The honor is presented annually to support the career of a visual artist or visual artist collaborators living and working in the Greater Baltimore region in USA. Thea has a conceptual, research-driven practice that examines Philippine identity through craft and material histories, sculptural objects, textiles, installations, and digital media. Her work also considers how Philippine materials and cultural forms are represented and transformed through migration and diaspora. The artist earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Fibers from the Maryland Institute College of Art in 2006 and a Master of Fine Arts from Emily Carr University of Art and Design in Vancouver in 2023. She works as a studio artist, freelance designer, and educator. Thea lives in Baltimore with her husband, David, and their son, Isagani. Her research has taken her to the Philippines and Spain, where, as a Jacques and Natasha Gelman Travel Fellow, she studied Spanish colonial-era archives and textile collections. She also spent a year researching Indigenous textile weaving practices in the Philippines, work that informed her investigations into colonial economies and the country’s history of labor migration. The recognition comes two years after Thea was selected as a semifinalist for the Sondheim Art Prize in 2024. This year, she was one of five finalists, alongside Leigh Davis, Brandon Donahue-Shipp, Curran Hatleberg, and Danni O’Brien. Works by the five finalists are currently featured in the Janet and Walter Sondheim Art Prize Finalists Exhibition at the Walters Art Museum’s Hackerman House. The exhibition, which opened June 25, runs through Sept. 13.

What Filinvest City reveals about the future of business districts. As hybrid work reshapes employee expectations and labor markets become more competitive, companies are taking a broader view of what a business address needs to provide. Increasingly, businesses are evaluating whether their location can support workforce needs, future growth, and continuity over the long term. This shift has increased the importance of the business district itself, with companies placing greater emphasis on the strength and completeness of their surrounding ecosystem. In Alabang, Filinvest City offers a compelling case. Spanning 244 hectares, the master-planned garden CBD of the Metro South has grown into one of the country's most established business locations by integrating workplaces, residences, healthcare facilities, educational institutions, retail destinations, hospitality offerings, and public spaces within a single urban environment. With limited commercial lots remaining, Filinvest City continues to welcome businesses and investors seeking to build within a proven business district supported by decades of development, strong market confidence, and sustained growth. The advantage now lies in both proximity and functionality. Daily needs that would typically require travel across multiple locations are concentrated within the district, allowing employees and businesses to operate within a more connected setting. The result is an environment designed to support both business activity and everyday life. Talent beyond the metro core The growing importance of geography is perhaps most evident in the competition for talent. As companies expand their hiring footprint beyond traditional business centers, accessibility has become a strategic consideration. The ability to draw from multiple labor markets can widen recruitment opportunities and provide greater flexibility as workforce requirements evolve. Filinvest City's location in Alabang positions it at the intersection of Metro Manila and Southern Luzon. Through major transport links including the South Luzon Expressway, the Skyway System, the Muntinlupa-Cavite Expressway, with the future railway system set to enhance regional connectivity, businesses can access talent pools that extend across Muntinlupa, Las Piñas, Parañaque, Cavite, Laguna, and Batangas. For employers, that reach can translate into a wider pipeline of professionals and a reduced reliance on a single labor market. In an environment where workforce availability increasingly influences business performance, connectivity becomes more than an infrastructure feature. It becomes an operational asset. The value of a proven district Corporate tenants are also paying closer attention to the maturity of the locations in which they operate. Filinvest City's growth has been supported by measurable market performance over the past decade. Land values within the district have increased by 346 percent, equivalent to a 17 percent compounded annual growth rate, reflecting sustained demand driven by real business activity and long-term investor confidence. Commercial land that traded at approximately ₱50,000 per square meter in 2010 now commands prices approaching ₱500,000 per square meter. Beyond valuation growth, the district has matured into a fully operational urban center, with approximately 19 million sqm of gross floor area already delivered, and daily foot traffic estimated at 220,000 people. Its appeal is further evidenced by the presence of major locators such as PLDT, SONAK, and Pepsi, whose investments underscore Filinvest City's role as an established business destination. The township remains the first and only LEED- and BERDE-certified central business district in the Philippines.
